statement: The SOA curve has four regions: maximum current at low VCE, a thermally limited region, a second-breakdown region, and breakdown voltage.
locator: SAFE OPERATING AREA, first four paragraphs

statement: The SOA curve is an absolute maximum rating; operating on the thermal-limit portion produces the maximum allowable junction temperature and is not advised for long-term operation, while operation below the limit improves reliability and MTTF.
locator: SAFE OPERATING AREA, paragraphs after the four regions

statement: For a DC resistive load, peak amplifier dissipation occurs at an output voltage of V+/2, or 50% output, where PD = (V+)^2/(4RL).
For a sine wave, amplifier dissipation reaches a maximum when the output peaks are about 63% of the supply voltage, because the instantaneous output remains near half-supply for much of the cycle.
A purely reactive load delivers zero power, so the amplifier dissipates all the power drawn from the supply; at full output this is about three times the worst-case dissipation with a resistive load.

A short to ground forces the full supply across the conducting output transistor; with +/-40 V, a 3 A current limit is safe only if the case is held at 25 C and dissipates 120 W, while an 85 C case allows 2 A and 80 W with a 0.75 C/W heatsink.
A short to either supply puts the sum of both supply voltages across the output transistor, a more demanding case than a short to ground.
A foldover current limiter reduces the current limit when VCE is high, but it can produce unusual behavior with reactive loads.

AC signals are generally less demanding than DC signals of the same peak voltage and current because above about 50 Hz the junction temperature follows average power, and in a bipolar sine wave each output transistor rests for a half-cycle.
A transistor's maximum dissipation rating applies at a 25 C case and derates linearly to zero at about 150 C; very few transistors are designed for a junction temperature above 150 C.
For a 150 C device the derating factor is the 25 C dissipation divided by 125 C; a 230 W device therefore derates by 1.84 W/C.
In ESP's example, Rth(j-c) = 0.54 C/W, Rth(c-h) = 1 C/W and Rth(h-a) = 4 C/W, so 20 W continuous produces a 110 C die rise; at 25 C ambient the die is about 135 C.
A nominal 8 Ohm loudspeaker may fall to 3 Ohm or less and rise to 50 Ohm or more at driver resonance, and a nominal 4 Ohm loudspeaker may have a minimum near 3 Ohm.
At a 45 degree load phase angle, peak transistor dissipation doubles and power delivered to the load is halved; this is the worst case.
For a 3 Ohm load with 45 degree phase at +/-35 V, peak transistor dissipation is almost 200 W and average dissipation about 43 W; the peak occurs at the voltage zero crossing.
Second breakdown is a localized thermal runaway in a BJT that can destroy the device in about 10 ms while the case is still cool.
A 230 W transistor may be limited to about 120 W at typical operating temperatures because the junction-to-ambient thermal resistance is about 1.5-2 C/W even with a large heatsink.

MOSFETs do not suffer second breakdown, but switching (vertical) MOSFETs are not recommended for linear use; lateral MOSFETs are limited mainly by average power and can self-limit, although this is not a protection scheme.

A typical discrete SOA protection circuit senses current through the emitter resistors and removes base drive from the driver transistors; it must allow the high current that a reactive load demands at zero output voltage.
Fuses protect against fire and further damage, not the output devices: no fuse is fast enough to protect a transistor unless it is so low in value that it blows during normal use.

A protection circuit that switches the output devices off quickly can generate a destructive flyback voltage from a reactive load; catch diodes from the output to each supply clamp the output to the rails.
For a top-mounted heatsink the simplified thermal model is theta-JA = theta-JC + theta-CH + theta-HA and theta-JA = (TJ - TA)/PD.
In TI's example, 80 W into 4 Ohm dissipates about 13.6 W; with theta-JC = 0.6 C/W, TJ no more than 130 C and TA = 75 C, the case-to-ambient path must be no more than 3.44 C/W.
locator: 3.5 Thermal Interface Material and Heatsink, equations 3-4

statement: Class-D amplifiers achieve higher efficiency than Class-AB, but their power loss is not negligible and needs a PCB or heatsink thermal path; an inadequate thermal design can trigger thermal protection.

Audio thermal tests commonly use sine, pink noise or music; sine is the most strenuous and least representative, pink noise better simulates music's dynamic range, and automotive thermal tests typically use 75-85 C ambient.
The thermal design limit should be an overtemperature warning threshold rather than the shutdown threshold, because shutdown interrupts playback.
Increasing heatsink surface area reduces thermal resistance; theta-JA = 1/(hc A), so the resistance also falls when natural convection is replaced by forced convection.
The junction-to-ambient thermal resistance through a heatsink is theta-JC + theta-CS + theta-SA, so the interface material and heatsink resistances must both be minimized.
A heatsink's thermal resistance varies with power level, orientation and airflow, so its datasheet rating must be read for the actual mounting and flow conditions.
In natural convection, place heat sources near the top of the enclosure, avoid temperature-sensitive circuits above them, and orient heatsinks so air can pass freely over all fins.
Component reliability falls as junction temperature rises; Apex's normalized failure-rate curve is based on MIL-HDBK-217F and increases with temperature.
A shorted output transistor can put a rail voltage across the speaker; a 42 V DC fault into a 6 Ohm voice coil dissipates about 294 W continuously and can destroy the driver in seconds.
locator: DC offset and protection, first paragraphs

statement: A speaker-protection relay should short the speaker to ground when it operates rather than simply open the circuit, because a 70 V DC fault can sustain an arc across opening contacts.
Most common relays are rated 30 V DC at 10 A; two contact sets in series can interrupt about 60 V DC, and a 70 V DC arc may require at least 1.6 mm contact clearance.
locator: Relay Failure and DC offset sections

statement: A DC detector needs a low-frequency filter so legitimate low-frequency signals do not trip it; ESP uses a 1 Hz single-pole filter and reports that 30 V RMS at 5 Hz does not trigger it while 30 V DC triggers in 60 ms.
A relay coil driven through a catch diode releases more slowly; ESP measured 1.2 ms without a diode, 7.2 ms with a diode, and 3.5 ms with a diode-resistor network.
ESP recommends a MOSFET relay above +/-35 V because an electromechanical relay cannot reliably break the resulting DC arc.
Music crest factor can be as low as 6 dB and as high as 20 dB, a 100:1 power ratio; a 10 dB crest factor is a common assumption.
For electronics, ambient temperature is the temperature of the air surrounding the equipment at its hottest point, not the room temperature; an enclosed cabinet can reach 50 C when the room is 25 C.
An electrically isolating Kapton washer adds roughly twice the thermal resistance of a direct or grease-coupled joint.

Few discrete protection circuits monitor output-device temperature or average power, so a hot amplifier has less protection than a cold one; thermal tracking is automatic in IC power amplifiers because the devices share one die.
ESP states that +/-100 mV is generally accepted as the maximum DC offset, corresponding to 2.5 mW into a 4 Ohm load.
For a full-range system with a 20 Hz low-frequency limit, at least 25 ms of detection delay is needed to avoid nuisance tripping; practical systems often need more.
Speaker-cable resistance can mitigate the inductive part of a difficult load, but it wastes power and changes the load the amplifier sees.
Driver transistors are exposed to the same SOA limits as output devices and must be checked too.
Removing the relay catch diode gives the fastest release but produces a large back-EMF that can destroy the driver transistor; a diode-resistor network is a compromise.
